title: Behavior and adoptability of hoarded cats admitted to an animal shelter
authors: Jacobson LS, Ellis JJ, Janke KJ, Giacinti JA, Robertson JV
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: The study examined behavioral characteristics and adoption success for previously hoarded cats. Researchers analyzed shelter records and post-adoption surveys from 195 hoarded cats (≥6 months old at intake), of which 174 were adopted. Key findings included: 52% scored as 'friendly' at intake; socialization scores showed 87% were 'supersocial' or 'social' after shelter habituation, declining to 47% immediately post-adoption, then recovering to 84% more than a week after adoption. Most cats scoring 'tense' at intake showed improved socialization later. Out-of-box elimination was uncommon (only 1 of 88 cats exhibited it in both settings). Adopters expressed positive feelings for 42 of 43 cats surveyed. Return rates did not differ significantly between hoarded (10%) and non-hoarded (7.1%) cats, nor did behavioral return reasons. The authors conclude that hoarded cats demonstrated high adoptability and adoption satisfaction, suggesting behavior-based decisions should be deferred to allow habituation time.

title: Outbreak management of multidrug-resistant Bordetella bronchiseptica in 16 shelter-housed cats
authors: Rodriguez L, Berliner EA
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: This case series examines an outbreak of multidrug-resistant Bordetella bronchiseptica affecting 16 shelter cats with respiratory illness. Four cats presented with acute breathing difficulty, each with prior upper respiratory disease history. Early diagnostic testing and culture and sensitivity allowed for targeted antimicrobial therapy and environmental interventions. Twelve additional presumptive cases were identified using exposure and clinical criteria. The comprehensive response included diagnostic protocols, risk evaluation, vaccination, isolation measures, heightened monitoring, and biosecurity review. The outbreak resolved within 26 days. The study notes this represents the first documented management of an MDR Bordetella bronchiseptica outbreak in shelter cats. The authors emphasize that early use of necropsy, PCR testing, and bacterial culture enabled rapid deployment of effective second-line antibiotics, and stress the importance of outbreak expertise and antimicrobial stewardship in resource-limited shelter settings.

title: Diagnostic testing for feline panleukopenia in a shelter setting: a prospective, observational study
authors: Jacobson LS, Janke KJ, Giacinti J, Weese JS
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: This shelter-based investigation evaluated diagnostic approaches for feline panleukopenia virus (FPV) infection. Researchers compared point-of-care SNAP testing with quantitative real-time PCR, assessed alternative sample types (vomit, swabs), and clarified interpretation of weak-positive results. Among 145 cats, 17 had confirmed FPV infection and 62 tested negative. Fecal SNAP sensitivity reached 55%, while vomit PCR achieved 100% (n=17; 95% CI 16-100). Overall specificity remained high across all methods (96-100%). The analysis revealed that positive SNAP results, including weak positives, correlated with higher viral copy numbers than false-negative results. The authors conclude that SNAP testing functions as an initial screening tool. Positive fecal results—including weak positives—are reliable indicators in symptomatic animals, but negative results require PCR confirmation before ruling out FPV infection.

title: Fecal viral DNA shedding following clinical panleukopenia virus infection in shelter kittens: a prospective, observational study
authors: Janke KJ, Jacobson LS, Giacinti JA, Weese JS
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: The research investigated the extent and timeline of fecal viral DNA shedding in shelter cats diagnosed with feline panleukopenia using quantitative real-time PCR. Researchers followed 40 cats and kittens over a 21-day period, testing fecal samples on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 21. Key findings indicated that median DNA viral copy numbers fell below the diagnostic cut-off by day 7 with decreasing PCR positivity rates across the observation period. The study found that SNAP test results, diarrhea and systemic signs were inconsistent in relation to qPCR positivity. The authors recommended that infected cats should remain isolated for at least 14 days following diagnosis, after which release could be considered as part of a comprehensive infection control approach.

title: Effect of a provincial feline onychectomy ban on cat intake and euthanasia in a British Columbia animal shelter system
authors: Ellis A, van Haaften K, Protopopova A, Gordon E
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: This research examined whether a provincial ban on elective cat declawing affected shelter intake and euthanasia outcomes. The study analyzed British Columbia SPCA records from 36 months before (May 2015–April 2018; n=41,157) and after (May 2018–April 2021; n=33,430) the provincial ban on onychectomy. Destructive behavior was found to be an uncommon reason for surrender (0.18% of surrendered cats) during the study period. There was no statistically significant difference in the number of cats surrendered for destructive scratching behavior after the provincial ban on elective onychectomy. The proportion of owner-requested euthanasias decreased after the ban. The total number of cats surrendered, the shelter live release rate and average length of stay all remained stable or improved following the ban, though causation could not be determined.

title: Guidance for management of free-roaming community cats: a bioeconomic analysis
authors: Benka VA, Boone JD, Miller PS, Briggs JR, Anderson AM, Slootmaker C, Slater M, Levy JK, Nutter FB, Zawistowski S
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: This study employed computer modeling to evaluate various free-roaming cat management approaches and their expense-effectiveness. The research examined lethal removal, non-lethal removal, trap-neuter-return, combination strategies, and no intervention using stochastic simulation. Results indicated that cost-effective reduction of free-roaming cat numbers required sufficient management intensity, regardless of management approach. The findings showed removal produced faster initial population declines, though sterilization-based methods proved potentially more economical at higher intensities. Among five scenarios achieving comparable 45% population reductions, strategies emphasizing sterilization cost substantially less than removal-only approaches, offering communities evidence-based frameworks for developing informed management policies.

title: Ear-tipping practices for identification of cats sterilized in trap-neuter-return programs in the USA
authors: Dalrymple AM, MacDonald LJ, Kreisler RE
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: This study examined ear-tipping practices used in trap-neuter-return (TNR) programs across the USA. The researchers distributed an anonymous survey to 526 TNR program participants between October 4-20, 2021, with 410 completing it. Results showed that nearly all respondents recognized the ear tip as indicating sterilization, though some associated it with rabies vaccination or socialization status. Most practitioners tipped the left ear (81%) using visual estimation (92%), preferring a straight-across silhouette. The median post-hemostasis bleeding rate was 5%, with median negative feedback at 1%. The most common complaint involved removing excessive ear tissue. The study found significant variation in techniques without clear superior methods, concluding that standards for this procedure would be helpful.

title: Characteristics of cat semi-owners
authors: Ma GC, McLeod LJ, Zito SJ
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: The study examined people who care for stray cats without considering themselves owners. Researchers surveyed 8,708 New South Wales residents, finding that 588 respondents (7%) were 'semi-owners' of unowned cats. These individuals were significantly more likely to be female, urban-dwelling, from lower socioeconomic areas, and renting their homes. Notably, most semi-owners also owned their own cats and had more cats than non-semi-owners. The researchers concluded that semi-owners represent an important target audience for behavior change interventions aimed at managing cat populations, but interventions must acknowledge barriers like cost and trust issues.

title: Feline chaphamaparvovirus (feline fechavirus) in different cat populations
authors: Weese JS, MacNicol J
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: The researchers assessed the presence of feline chaphamaparvovirus (FeChPV) across various feline populations. They gathered fecal and vomitus samples from 136 cats across multiple facilities: 65 from a shelter without apparent gastrointestinal disease, 25 from shelters experiencing vomiting/diarrhea clusters, and 46 from a research colony following a recent outbreak. Testing revealed FeChPV in 30 of 136 samples (22%). Infection rates varied by location: 12% in the asymptomatic shelter, 11-25% in affected shelters, and 88% in one shelter with acute disease. Notably, the virus appeared in both symptomatic cats (33% of diarrheic animals) and healthy ones (17% of non-symptomatic cats). The researchers concluded that while FeChPV correlates with facility outbreaks, its precise pathogenic role remains ambiguous since detection occurred in healthy populations.

title: Effects of intranasal maropitant on clinical signs of naturally acquired upper respiratory disease in shelter cats
authors: Parncutt J, Johnson LR, Subharat S, Oke B, Hill KE
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: The research team investigated whether intranasal maropitant citrate could reduce severity of feline upper respiratory disease (FURD) in shelter settings. Sixty-one cats received either intranasal maropitant (34 cats) or saline placebo (27 cats) twice daily for seven days. Clinical assessments measured conjunctivitis, blepharospasm, ocular discharge, and nasal discharge using visual analogue scales at baseline and completion. Key finding: there was no significant difference in clinical index scores between the maropitant treatment and control groups for conjunctivitis, blepharospasm, ocular discharge, nasal discharge or total disease severity after 7 days. The researchers concluded that intranasal maropitant showed no clinical benefit compared to saline treatment, and found no evidence to support the routine use of intranasal maropitant in managing feline upper respiratory disease.

title: Randomized, non-inferiority clinical trial of three topical dermatophytosis treatments in shelter cats
authors: DeTar L, Janke KJ, Jacobson L
journal: Journal of Feline Medicine and Surgery
abstract: This prospective randomized trial evaluated three topical antifungal treatments for cats with Microsporum canis infections in shelter settings. All cats received oral itraconazole while being assigned to one of three topical groups: lime sulfur (LS), miconazole chlorhexidine (MC), or hydrogen peroxide (HP) shampoo. The study enrolled 76 cats across four US shelters. Lime sulfur significantly outperformed alternatives, achieving mycological cure by 7 weeks in all treated cats, compared to 62.5% of MC-treated and 78.3% of HP-treated cats. Mean time to cure was 27 days for LS versus 37 days for MC and 36 days for HP. Younger cats required longer treatment periods. Staff noted no meaningful differences between products regarding application difficulty or feline tolerance, though some side effects were documented including bleached hair (HP) and hypothermia (MC and HP). The researchers concluded that while LS demonstrated superior efficacy, hydrogen peroxide represents an acceptable alternative to lime sulfur if preferred.

title: The effect of animal shelter sound on cat behaviour and welfare
authors: Eagan BH, Gordon E, Fraser D
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: This investigation assessed how sound affected fear- and maintenance-related behaviors in single-housed shelter cats. Two daily 30-minute observation sessions (morning and evening) occurred for 98 cats over ten days. Cat behaviour and presence of sound (classified by source) were recorded by instantaneous and one-zero sampling with 15-second intervals. Sessions were classified as 'quiet' or 'noisy' based on median sound levels. Statistical analysis included 70 cats with adequate comparable observations. Males demonstrated less fear and maintenance behavior than females. Morning sessions consistently had much more sound than evenings, and cats showed more fear behaviour and less maintenance behaviour in the mornings. Cats exhibited more fear responses during noisy morning sessions compared to quiet ones. When sound transitioned from quiet to noisy, fear-related behaviour increased; transitions from noisy to quiet showed decreased fear behaviours. The findings indicate that shelter cats vary significantly in responsiveness, and environmental sound substantially influences their conduct. The researchers conclude that reducing shelter noise levels may enhance overall welfare outcomes for cats.

title: Animal sheltering: A scoping literature review grounded in institutional ethnography
authors: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: The authors examined research on animal sheltering through an institutional ethnography lens, focusing on actual work practices. They reviewed literature on three main areas: shelter staff experiences, animal relinquishment, and length of stay in shelters. Key findings reveal that euthanasia-related stress dominates research on staff, yet focus group participants emphasized decision-making tensions rather than the act itself. Research on relinquishment relies heavily on surveys and database records with significant limitations. Length of stay studies focus on animal characteristics like breed and color, overlooking actual work processes like veterinary treatment and behavioral modification. The authors conclude that institutional ethnography offers valuable insights by examining concrete work activities that current quantitative approaches overlook, potentially leading to better support for both animals and staff.

title: Using institutional ethnography to analyse animal sheltering and protection I: Animal protection work
authors: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: Animal protection enforcement in Canada relies on citizens reporting concerns, yet the actual work processes of law enforcement have received minimal scholarly attention. This study employed institutional ethnography to examine the daily activities of call centre operators and animal protection officers. The research revealed that staff attempt to identify evidence of animal 'distress' as legally defined, though many cases—such as animals in isolated or deprived situations—fall short of this definition, preventing intervention. Officers face constraints from privacy and property law requirements, and must document compliance attempts to justify further action including search warrants. These limitations can delay or prevent beneficial intervention. Officers sometimes work creatively to advocate for animals when legal tools prove insufficient. The study recommends expanding the legal definition of distress to better address animals' needs, developing broader intervention options for officers, and conducting ethnographic research across jurisdictions with different legal frameworks to understand how laws and policies organize animal protection work.

mcqs.e: The abstract states 'many cases—such as animals in isolated or deprived situations—fall short of this definition [of legal distress], preventing intervention,' limiting officers' ability to help animals who are clearly suffering.

mcqs.e: The abstract recommends 'expanding the legal definition of distress to better address animals' needs, developing broader intervention options for officers,' as the current definition prevents intervention in many cases of animal deprivation.

mcqs.e: The abstract states 'officers face constraints from privacy and property law requirements, and must document compliance attempts to justify further action including search warrants,' creating procedural barriers that can delay beneficial intervention.

title: Using institutional ethnography to analyse animal sheltering and protection II: Animal shelter work
authors: Koralesky KE, Rankin JM, Fraser D
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: The study employed institutional ethnography to examine how frontline shelter staff's daily activities connect to standardized organizational procedures at a large animal protection organization. Staff regularly perform behavioral assessments and review intake documents to guide animal care and inform potential adopters while safeguarding volunteers and the public. However, staff faced significant time constraints and pressure when working with behaviorally challenged animals because their efforts were primarily directed toward facilitating quick adoptions for most animals and preparing for future kennel space demands. Management systems focused on maintaining manageable animal populations based on available resources, reducing shelter duration, and individualized housing. These systems ultimately limited staff's capacity to provide intensive behavioral work for long-stay animals with serious problems. This situation created occupational stress for caregiving staff who felt emotionally invested in these animals' outcomes. The researchers recommend exploring behavioral modification support and expanding foster programs for animals with specialized needs.

o: Staff wanted to euthanize difficult animals but management required adoption efforts

mcqs.e: The abstract states 'staff faced significant time constraints and pressure when working with behaviorally challenged animals because their efforts were primarily directed toward facilitating quick adoptions for most animals and preparing for future kennel space demands.'

mcqs.q: According to Koralesky et al. 2023 (Part II), what did management systems in the studied shelter organization prioritize?

mcqs.e: The abstract states 'management systems focused on maintaining manageable animal populations based on available resources, reducing shelter duration, and individualized housing,' which created systemic constraints on behavioral support for difficult animals.

mcqs.q: What recommendations did Koralesky et al. 2023 (Part II) make based on their institutional ethnography of shelter work?

mcqs.e: The abstract recommends 'exploring behavioral modification support and expanding foster programs for animals with specialized needs,' to address the structural limitation that prevented intensive work with difficult long-stay animals.

title: Predictors of successful diversion of cats and dogs away from animal shelter intake: Analysis of data from a self-rehoming website
authors: Ly LH, Protopopova A
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: As animals experience distress in animal shelters, leaders call for increased efforts to divert intake of companion animals away from shelters. One novel intake diversion strategy is supported self-rehoming, where owners find new homes for their animals without surrendering to a physical shelter. This study aimed to identify predictors of successful diversion of animals through the AdoptaPet.com 'Rehome' online platform. Data for dogs (n=100,342) and cats (n=48,484) were analysed through logistic regression to assess the association of animal- and owner-related factors and outcome. Overall, 87.1% of dogs and 85.7% of cats were successfully diverted from animal shelters, out of which, 37.8% of dogs and 35.3% of cats were kept by their original owner. Multiple animal-related factors predicted increased odds of diversion (e.g. younger, smaller). Dog and cat owners who set a longer rehoming deadline (i.e. >8 weeks) were over twice as likely to keep or adopt out their animal. Dog owners who surrendered for owner-related reasons had increased odds of diversion in comparison to animal behaviour issues. We conclude that online-supported, self-rehoming platforms provide pet owners with an alternative to relinquishment that may reduce the intake of animals to shelters; however, owners with animals that are not preferred by adopters may have to decide whether to keep their animal or relinquish their animal to a shelter or rescue.

mcqs.e: The abstract states 'Overall, 87.1% of dogs and 85.7% of cats were successfully diverted from animal shelters,' suggesting self-rehoming platforms are highly effective at keeping animals out of shelters when owners are motivated to use them.

mcqs.e: The abstract states 'Dog and cat owners who set a longer rehoming deadline (i.e. >8 weeks) were over twice as likely to keep or adopt out their animal,' suggesting that more time enables successful placement.

mcqs.q: What limitation of self-rehoming platforms did Ly and Protopopova 2023 identify regarding animals less preferred by adopters?

mcqs.e: The abstract concludes 'owners with animals that are not preferred by adopters may have to decide whether to keep their animal or relinquish their animal to a shelter or rescue,' recognizing the platform's limitation for harder-to-place animals.

title: Companion animal adoption and relinquishment during the COVID-19 pandemic: The experiences of animal rescue staff and volunteers
authors: Carroll GA, Reeve C, Torjussen A
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: There has been a paucity of research into the experiences of animal rescue staff and volunteers during COVID-19. The aim of this qualitative research was to explore the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on companion animal rescue organisations and their staff and volunteers, and to develop a set of recommendations on how to reduce the risk to companion animal welfare during a crisis. Descriptive thematic analysis was used to explore the experiences of staff and volunteers from 28 animal rescue organisations, most of which were based in the UK. Other surveyed countries included Germany, the Republic of Ireland, France, Spain, the USA and Australia. We identify three key themes that reflect the challenges faced by pet rescue organisations during the pandemic: (1) impact on animals; (2) impact on identity; and (3) impact on organisational processes. Key recommendations include the promotion of co-operation and modifications within the sector, the need to understand, and change, detrimental pet-owner behaviours, and the need to clarify the identity of animal rescue organisations within the Government. Both positive and negative outcomes were experienced by animal rescue organisations during the COVID-19 pandemic. These findings should be considered for future crises and indeed the everyday operating procedures of companion animal rescue organisations.

mcqs.e: The abstract states 'We identify three key themes that reflect the challenges faced by pet rescue organisations during the pandemic: (1) impact on animals; (2) impact on identity; and (3) impact on organisational processes.'

mcqs.e: The abstract states key recommendations include 'the promotion of co-operation and modifications within the sector, the need to understand, and change, detrimental pet-owner behaviours,' and clarifying rescue identity within Government.

mcqs.q: What study design did Carroll et al. 2024 use to explore animal rescue staff and volunteer experiences during COVID-19?
o: A randomized controlled trial comparing shelter management strategies

mcqs.e: The abstract states 'Descriptive thematic analysis was used to explore the experiences of staff and volunteers from 28 animal rescue organisations,' a qualitative approach suited to understanding lived experiences during the pandemic.

title: Companion animal adoption and relinquishment during the COVID-19 pandemic: Households with children at greatest risk of relinquishing a cat or dog
authors: Carroll GA, Torjussen A, Reeve C
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: The study examined factors linked to pet relinquishment during COVID-19 across multiple countries. Researchers surveyed 3,945 pet owners and identified that households with children were 4.6 times more likely to consider or have already relinquished a cat or dog compared to those without children. Additional risk factors included male pet ownership and younger animal age. Notably, the analysis found no association between online acquisition source and relinquishment risk. Among those who relinquished pets, 76.2% found the decision emotionally difficult, though all agreed it was logically correct. The USA showed significantly higher relinquishment rates than the UK and Italy. The research highlights the need for targeted interventions supporting families with children in pet retention.

title: Shelter and rescue programmes associated with higher live release and lower return rates for dogs
authors: Reese LA
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: The research examines how shelter characteristics and initiatives affect positive outcomes for dogs. Drawing on survey data from 370 U.S. animal shelters and rescues, the study identifies three key factors associated with improved results: avoiding breed designations for mixed-breed dogs, maintaining robust foster networks, and implementing matching systems. The findings indicate that it is the programmes shelters and rescues implement, not simply their human and financial resources, that are associated with positive outcomes.

title: The role of breed and personality descriptions in influencing perceptions of shelter dog adoptability
authors: Archer C, Hall NJ, Andrukonis A
journal: Animal Welfare
abstract: The study examined how breed labels and personality descriptions affect potential adopters' likelihood of choosing shelter dogs. Researchers presented dog photographs to participants under four conditions: photo alone, photo with breed identification, photo with personality traits, and photo with both elements combined. Key findings indicate that descriptions significantly increased perceived adoptability, while breed labels decreased it. Specific breed designations like Chihuahua mix, Chow mix, and Jack Russell Terrier mix negatively influenced adoption interest, whereas 'Lab mix' improved ratings. Personality descriptors such as affectionate, calm, and friendly boosted perceived adoptability; notably, 'energetic' reduced adoption interest. The research suggests removing breed labels and incorporating positive personality descriptions could enhance adoption outcomes and potentially reduce how long dogs remain in shelters, thereby supporting animal welfare objectives.

title: Shelter Worker's Experiences and Perceptions of Capacity for Care (C4C)
authors: Hobson S, Bateman S, Coe JB, Oblak ML
journal: Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science
abstract: Capacity for Care (C4C) is a shelter population management strategy which utilizes managed intake to optimize in-shelter populations based on housing capacity and available resources. The purpose of this study was to (1) understand staff experiences using managed intake, (2) explore staff perceptions of how the C4C model has been regarded by other staff at their facility, and (3) explore the response of community members who are attempting to relinquish their cats, as perceived by the staff who are communicating with cat owners and scheduling relinquishment. Participants recruited from shelters who practiced C4C participated in a semi-structured interview and completed a written survey to share their experiences and perceptions of C4C. Based on the perceptions of the participants, evidence suggests the waitlist may decrease the admission of owned cats to the shelter as a result of advising cat owners about alternatives to relinquishment. Additional investigation would help clarify how managed intake affects community cats awaiting shelter admission.

title: Community factors and animal shelter outcomes
authors: Reese LA
journal: Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science
abstract: This research explores connections between the nature of a community, the type of animal shelter it has, how animals arrive at the shelter, and outcomes for the animals in terms of adoption or euthanasia. Based on data from Shelter Animals Count, the study concludes that the nature of the local community is related to the type of shelter it is served by, how dogs arrive at the shelter, and directly to outcomes. Areas with greater economic stress and lower educational attainment are more likely to have a municipal shelter, which increases stray intake, and ultimately euthanasia. Community economic stress is also directly associated with lower adoption and higher euthanasia rates. The findings of the study suggest a multi-pronged strategy to increase adoptions and reduce euthanasia focusing on both animal shelters but also using a One Health approach to improve the welfare of both humans and non-human animals.

title: Attitudes Toward Spay/Neuter in the US Population: Urban/Rural, Cat/Dog, and Demographic Differences
authors: Glasser CL
journal: Anthrozoös
abstract: An online survey of 991 US adults examines differences in attitudes among the general US population toward spaying and neutering cats and dogs, with a focus on differences between urban and rural respondents and the influence of demographic characteristics. Twelve items measure attitudes toward spay/neuter. Each item is analyzed with a separate multiple regression to understand urban–rural, cat–dog and demographic differences in attitudes. Results indicate fewer urban–rural and cat–dog differences than expected, though rural respondents are less likely to find the practice cruel, think animals should have a litter before sterilization, or support laws to require sterilization. People asked about dogs are more likely to agree that spay/neuter operations are expensive but are less likely to believe it is the right thing to do than those asked about cats. The most prevalent characteristics impacting attitudes are guardianship, age, and gender, with guardians more likely to attribute positive health and behavioral outcomes to sterilization and feel that it is morally and socially positive.
